title: Pizarro 1532–1533: research edition
scope: An open research dossier of the main march, subsidiary journeys, source testimony and unresolved questions.
summary: Seventeen legacy entries have been audited. A ten-event core, twenty-three additional source-index entries and six regional cultural contexts are presented for discussion. Seven Motux statements have independent editorial review; this is not a complete or historically certified reconstruction.
notice: Reviewed facts, source-backed proposals and documented gaps retain different statuses. Modern references and photographs do not identify exact historical camps. Publication for discussion does not upgrade the underlying research findings.

sections.title: Scope
sections.summary: A proposed main march from Tumbez to Cuzco in 1532–1533, with three subsidiary or returning journeys kept separate.

sections.title: Itinerary
sections.summary: Ten core events and twenty-three additional source-index entries are available for comparison with all seventeen legacy records, including the duplicated Motux entries. Intermediate historical locations remain unresolved.
gaps: The legacy route mixes main travel, side expeditions, repeated places and city events. A human scope decision and reviewed mapping are still required.
Markham identifies Motux with Motupe, but the supplied sources do not establish exact historic camp coordinates. The modern Motupe point is a reference marker only.

sections.title: Chronology
sections.summary: Dates retain their supported day, month or year precision. The Motux passage gives four days of rest; its exact arrival date remains unknown. Partial dates do not become invented travel days.
gaps: The selected Xerez passage gives a four-day rest but no exact Motux arrival or departure date. Its narrative position falls after San Miguel departure24September1532 and before Caxamalca arrival15November1532.

sections.title: Sources
sections.summary: Testimony comes from Xerez and Sancho in English translations: Markham’s 1872 edition, consulted in a 1970 reprint, and Means’s 1917 edition. These are translated witnesses; no original Pizarro manuscript has been authenticated here.
gaps: The evidence is an1872 English translation preserved in a1970 reprint scan and pdftotext extraction with OCR artifacts. It is neither an autograph nor the original Spanish manuscript; Markham editorial notes remain separate from Xerez narrative.

sections.title: People and cultural context
sections.summary: Fourteen linked studies support six scoped regional context sections. Consultation levels, places and periods remain explicit; they do not establish the identities of people encountered at individual stops.
gaps: The supplied sources do not establish an ethnic or linguistic identity for the people encountered at Motux. General coastal-road descriptions and a later Mórrope study cannot provide that assignment.

sections.title: Images
sections.summary: Fifteen Commons records include three rejected place matches. One Motupe image has verified local bytes and visual inspection. Other candidates remain item links; all photographs serve modern or regional context.
gaps: Earlier original/thumbnail requests returned HTTP429/403. In the supervised 2026-10-23 Europe/Rome trial, one fresh metadata request and one original-image request succeeded (HTTP200); the retrieved JPEG matches the Commons-reported SHA1 and has been visually inspected. It supports modern-place context only. Exact capture date, camera GPS, independent rights-holder confirmation and correspondence with the historic Motux camp remain unverified.

sections.title: Narrative
sections.summary: Seven Motux statements retain their independently reviewed wording. The wider itinerary and cultural contexts remain documented editorial proposals for discussion.

sections.title: Review and open questions
sections.summary: Two bounded tasks have independent reviews: a documented arrival-date gap and a modern photo candidate. Six tasks await work and two depend on an editorial scope decision. No section or journey is certified complete.
gaps: The linked study was consulted at official bibliographic-record and abstract level. Its regional,later scope is relevant background only; it cannot be treated as direct testimony about Motux1532.

stages.modern_name: Tumbes / Cabeza de Vaca area, Peru
stages.event: Xerez reports that Pizarro reached Tumbez by sea and found its inhabitants armed. The expedition remained there before beginning its southward march on 16 May 1532. The map uses a modern reference near the archaeological area of Cabeza de Vaca; it does not identify the exact landing or camp.

date.note: The arrival took place before the departure explicitly dated 16 May 1532 in Xerez, p. 20. The checked narrative does not supply a secure arrival month or day. Modern archaeological reference point; precise landing and lodging unverified.

location.label: Approximate modern reference; exact historical site unverified.

stages.event: Xerez describes the foundation of San Miguel near Tangarara on the Chira River. The town provided a base before Pizarro departed to seek Atahualpa on 24 September 1532. Its modern village marker is distinct from present-day Piura and does not prove the precise location of the 1532 buildings.

date.note: The foundation is recorded in 1532 without an exact day in the checked narrative. The departure is explicitly dated 24 September 1532 in Xerez, p. 25. Modern Tangarará village coordinates are approximate references, not proof of the original town site.

location.label: Approximate modern reference; exact historical site unverified.

stages.modern_name: Jequetepeque valley approach to Cajamarca, Peru
stages.event: Hernando Pizarro names La Ramada in his account of the approach to Cajamarca. The route then changed from relatively flat country to difficult mountainous passes. Its association with the Jequetepeque valley is Markham’s later editorial identification; the map point is a regional approximation.

date.note: November 1532 is reconstructed from the sequence shortly before the explicitly dated 15 November arrival at Cajamarca. The editor’s itinerary gives 10 November for the ascent; the cited primary passage itself is undated. Exact La Ramada site and this regional map point remain unverified.

stages.event: Xerez dates Pizarro’s arrival at Cajamarca to the hour of vespers on 15 November 1532. He describes Atahualpa’s camp nearby and the Spaniards occupying the town’s open square. This records the governor’s arrival, before the capture of Atahualpa the following day.

stages.event: Sancho describes Pizarro and his horsemen entering Xauxa during the main march toward Cuzco in 1533. The governor remained to guard the town while other captains pursued forces across the river. This stage is distinct from earlier emissaries travelling through Xauxa and from Markham’s note about Huascar.

cultural_contexts.title: North coast / Tallán
cultural_contexts.text: The north coast should be introduced through its linguistic and political diversity. Arrizabalaga (2024) distinguishes Mochica, Sechura, Catacaos and Colán in later historical records, and challenges the influential idea that Sec united the entire Piura region. For seventeenth-century Catacaos and Sechura, Diez (2006) examines colonial caciques as local authorities whose legitimacy and obligations connected their communities with the colonial administration. Together these studies offer context for language and negotiated authority; they do not identify the language or ethnic membership of every person met by Pizarro in 1532.
cultural_contexts.period_limits: Arrizabalaga discusses Calancha (1638), Martínez Compañón (1783), and subsequent interpretation; Diez concerns the seventeenth century. Neither abstract establishes the identities or institutions of a specific 1532 encounter.
cultural_contexts.source_limits: Arrizabalaga explicitly criticizes regionalist reconstruction and later historiographical transmission. Diez analyzes authority under institutions imposed by the colonial regime; those institutions cannot be projected unchanged onto pre-conquest society.

cultural_contexts.title: Motupe / Lambayeque
cultural_contexts.text: For the Lambayeque region around Motupe, a useful later context is the study of everyday life after conquest rather than a single ethnic label. Klaus (2016) brings documentary, archaeological and biological evidence together at Mórrope to investigate colonial changes in health, diet, physical activity, burial practice and identity. He also warns that European interpretations can obscure indigenous experience. His work opens questions about bodies, food and community beyond the conquerors’ narrative, but concerns Mórrope in 1536–1750; its abstract supplies neither a description of Motux in 1532 nor specific results that can safely be transferred there.
cultural_contexts.period_limits: Study scope 1536–1750, Mórrope in Lambayeque. Mórrope and Motupe are different places; regional relevance is contextual, not a claim of identical populations or practices.
cultural_contexts.source_limits: Klaus explicitly discusses European ethnocentrism and misinterpretation. The abstract describes research questions and methods; no particular diet, disease rate or burial result is asserted here.

cultural_contexts.title: Cajamarca / Caxamarca
cultural_contexts.text: Cajamarca’s context includes political and linguistic histories that resist a uniform regional identity. Watanabe (2002), using Tantarica excavations and documents, reports stronger material connections with the north coast than with the Cajamarca valley and proposes that Cuismancu’s seven-waranga political unit formed under Inca rule. Andrade Ciudad (2010) likewise argues for successive linguistic strata, including Den and Culle, while warning against generalizing his model across Cajamarca. These are archaeological and linguistic interpretations of regional change, useful alongside the encounter narrative; neither establishes one ethnicity or language for everyone present at Cajamarca in 1532.
cultural_contexts.period_limits: Watanabe treats formation and transformation under the Inca state; Andrade proposes earlier linguistic strata. Neither abstract supplies an individual-level population identification at the 1532 encounter.
cultural_contexts.source_limits: Cuismancu formation and language strata are the authors’ interpretations, stated as proposals rather than settled universal facts. Andrade explicitly limits regional extrapolation.

cultural_contexts.title: Xauxa / Mantaro
cultural_contexts.text: For Xauxa and the Mantaro valley, household archaeology provides a perspective beyond imperial leaders. In his openly readable conclusion, D’Altroy (2002) describes the last pre-Inca century, the archaeological Wanka II phase, as marked by local competition and limited social differentiation; he contrasts it with greater regional peace and political hierarchy under Inca rule. Perales Munguía (2011) adds a historiographical caution: accounts of the valley’s past also participate in modern constructions of ethnicity. These perspectives frame farming households and changing political relations without turning an archaeological phase, a modern identity or a general alliance story into proof about every person encountered at Xauxa.
cultural_contexts.period_limits: D’Altroy contrasts pre-Inca and Inca household settings. Perales discusses modern historical memory. Wanka II is treated as an archaeological phase; no modern ethnography is used as evidence of 1533 custom.
cultural_contexts.source_limits: D’Altroy’s contrast is an archaeological synthesis. The readable Perales abstract supports the role of historical representation in modern ethnicity, but its opening alone does not prove every detailed claim about a supposed Huanca kingdom false.

cultural_contexts.title: Vilcas / Vilcashuamán
cultural_contexts.text: Vilcashuamán can be presented as a place with successive occupations rather than a timeless ethnic portrait. González Carré and Pozzi-Escot (2002) combine documents with ceramics and architecture to examine Late Intermediate Period settlement and subsequent Inca occupation. In a separate reassessment of colonial accounts, Santillana (2002) proposes several possible Chanca trajectories under Inca rule, including military incorporation, service to royal lineages and smaller settlements. His alternatives are hypotheses, not a census of Vilcas. Together the studies encourage a narrative about changing political arrangements and material life while leaving the identities of particular people in the 1533 encounter unassigned.
cultural_contexts.period_limits: Local Vilcashuamán occupation phases are distinct from Santillana’s wider reconstruction of Chanca distribution. No Andahuaylas-to-Vilcas identity equivalence is asserted.
cultural_contexts.source_limits: Santillana explicitly evaluates the quality of colonial sources and presents hypotheses. Terms for service and military incorporation in those sources require contextual reading, not a universal Chanca identity story.

cultural_contexts.title: Cusco region — explicitly later ethnographic comparison
cultural_contexts.text: A clearly dated ethnographic comparison can show a dimension of life in the wider Cusco region that conquest narratives overlook. Allen (1981) describes coca sharing in a Quechua-speaking community in Paucartambo: participants exchange leaves with invitations and thanks, and invoke spiritual beings. She interprets this etiquette as expressing ayllu, understood through common origin and relationships with sacred places. This concerns a modern community outside Cusco city. It offers a specific example of reciprocity and place-based belonging, not evidence that the same ceremony occurred at Pizarro’s arrival in 1533 or that all Quechua-speaking people shared identical customs.
cultural_contexts.period_limits: Published in 1981; fieldwork dates are not specified in the consulted abstract and are not invented. Paucartambo is distinct from Cusco city. No continuity claim to 1533 is established.
cultural_contexts.source_limits: The concepts are Allen’s ethnographic interpretation of one community; neither the study nor this paragraph speaks for all Quechua people. The abstract does not name the community, so this draft does not introduce a name from unverified secondary recollection.

legacy_rows.name: San Miguel
findings: The existing quotation is Markham’s commentary on earlier coastal reconnaissance and interpreters, not a San Miguel entry.
The founding settlement was at Tangarara on the Chira, rather than the modern city centre of Piura.
Tumbez precedes San Miguel. The primary narrative explicitly dates departure to 24 September 1532, rather than founding or arrival.

legacy_rows.name: Tumbez
findings: The October 1532 arrival contradicts the primary narrative’s departure from Tumbez on 16 May 1532.
This stop must precede San Miguel. The exact arrival month and day are not established by the checked passage.
The existing coordinate is not justified by a site-level source; a modern regional reference must not imply an exact historical landing.

legacy_rows.name: the Piura valley
findings: The existing quotation concerns intelligence received at San Miguel, rather than entry into the Piura valley.
Xerez describes arrival a few days after departure on 24 September; October is not the arrival month.
The editor’s itinerary gives 27 September, but its interpretation is not adopted as an exact primary date.

legacy_rows.name: Motux
findings: No quotation or event is present.
This and seq 5 duplicate the same place, coordinates and date. The source attests one four-day stay.
Motupe is Markham’s later identification, and an exact historical lodging is not located.

legacy_rows.name: Motux
findings: This is an exact duplicate of seq 4.
The source does not supply evidence of a second Motux stay. Merge the records and preserve the disposition in an audit.

legacy_rows.name: Guamamayo
findings: The quotation belongs to Astete’s account of Hernando Pizarro’s expedition in 1533, rather than Francisco’s main march in October 1532.
Markham identifies Guamamayo with La Barranca, not Pacasmayo.
Astete’s 9 January departure is corrected to 30 January by the editor; an exact day must retain this disagreement.
Keep this expedition separate from the main itinerary.

legacy_rows.name: La Ramada
findings: The existing excerpt is Markham’s footnote, rather than contemporary diary prose.
Hernando Pizarro’s letter directly names La Ramada on the approach to Cajamarca.
An October arrival is unsupported by the checked sequence; November is reconstructed from the approach to the 15 November arrival.
The Jequetepeque identification is editorial; the exact historic site remains unresolved.

legacy_rows.name: Caxas
findings: This is Soto’s subsidiary mission before Motux and La Ramada, not a later stage of the governor’s main march.
The editor’s itinerary places the dispatch in October; November is unsupported.
The excerpt ends mid-sentence. The exact Caxas site needs independent geographic identification.

legacy_rows.name: Huanca-pampa
findings: The quote describes Caxas and accidentally includes unrelated editorial footnotes.
Guacamba / Huanca-pampa is associated with northern Huancabamba on the Marañón watershed, not Huamachuco.
The latitude, longitude and November date are wrong for the described mission. Keep the stop in Soto’s separate branch.

legacy_rows.name: Caxamalca
findings: The primary narrative explicitly gives 15 November 1532.
Caxamalca and Cassamarca are variant names for Cajamarca in the editions.
The old paragraph carries OCR and footnote artifacts; replace it with a source-copied clean sentence and retain the dated context separately.

legacy_rows.name: Caxamalca
findings: The old excerpt ends within the word “declared”; the full quote fails token-boundary matching, while its complete-word prefix matches the source.
17 June 1533 is the date of Sancho’s certification and ransom accounting, rather than a new arrival.
Retain this as a city event at Cajamarca without inventing another travel leg.

legacy_rows.name: Pachacama
findings: The leader is Hernando Pizarro and the source author is Miguel de Astete.
The body says Sunday, 30 January; Markham’s note corrects it to Sunday, 5 February 1533.
The exact date is disputed in the supplied edition. Keep both readings explicit and place the stop in a separate branch before the June ransom accounting.

legacy_rows.name: Xauxa
findings: The existing quotation is Markham’s footnote about earlier emissaries and Huascar, not Francisco’s August arrival.
Sancho, Chapters III–IV, attests the main expedition at Xauxa during the later 1533 march.
The selected primary passage does not establish the former August month; use coarse dating and the correct narrative.

legacy_rows.name: Huanca-pampa
findings: The excerpt is copied from Soto’s Caxas mission in 1532 and does not describe Huancayo in September 1533.
Huanca-pampa has been incorrectly mapped a second time, here to Huancayo.
Sancho records travel down the Xauxa river valley, but this does not attest a stop at a town named Huancayo. Remove the town claim or represent an explicitly approximate regional passage.

legacy_rows.name: Vilcas
findings: No quotation or event is present.
Sancho, Chapter VIII, directly attests a stop at Bilcas between Xauxa and Cuzco.
Neither the former October date nor a proposed 4 November date is stated in the checked passage.
Identification with Vilcashuamán is later editorial geography, rather than primary numeric coordinates.

legacy_rows.name: Cuzco
findings: The existing Xerez excerpt describes an earlier messenger’s report, not the governor’s main entry into Cuzco.
The existing event incorrectly attributes the main entry to Hernando Pizarro.
Sancho, Chapter XI, explicitly dates the governor’s entry to 15 November 1533. The PDF page header is not narrative content.

legacy_rows.name: San Miguel
findings: The quotation is genuine Xerez, but its travellers are men returning home with their shares, not Francisco Pizarro.
December 1533 is not dated in the cited passage, which describes more than one departure.
A return to San Miguel must be kept as a distinct branch, and the original settlement must not be silently equated with present-day Piura.
